results.title: Coffee Break: Dolly Parton, the Dead Zone, Junk Food Addiction, and Algorithmic Intelligence
results.author: KLG
results.content:
Part the First: Dolly Parton, American from an Old School. August 2026 was the cruelest month for me in a long time. Dolly Parton died, to be closely followed by Wendell Berry. Mr. Berry will be a topic for next week. But this Friday we will remember Dolly Parton. For me, she goes back to the late-1960s when she was one of Porter Wagoner’s “girl singers” on his syndicated television show, which we watched on 19-inch black and white TV set hooked up to the original version of cable TV in which the signal was captured by a tall commercial antenna and transmitted to each subscribing house by copper cable. I was in junior high school, but Dolly was memorable.
Elizabeth Stice covers her uncommon virtues at Front Porch Republic (FPR) in Dolly Parton: A Woman of Many Virtues:
Like many long-lived celebrities, Dolly Parton went through several stages in public perception. She was once a “girl singer” for Porter Wagoner, then a country artist in her own right, then a pop star and sex symbol, and a sometime movie star. Her look was at different times considered chic, or cheap, or even camp. There have been a lot of jokes over the years. But in the last decade, she has been seen as a somewhat saintly figure and a person worthy of study. There are university history classes about her.
There will only ever be one Dolly Parton. But there are many ways to look at her legacy and her relationship to our country and its culture. And there are many things we can learn from her life.
One way of looking at Dolly Parton is through the lens of the American Dream, which she certainly achieved. She was born in rural Tennessee in 1946. Her father was a hard-working, illiterate sharecropper and the family lived in a one-room cabin. She had eleven siblings. Her song “Coat of Many Colors,” was based on her real-life experience of being so poor that she had a coat of rags sewn together one winter by her mother. As she sang, others teased her, “But they didn’t understand it, and I tried to make them see / One is only poor, only if they choose to be / Now I know we had no money, but I was rich as I could be / In my coat of many colors my momma made for me.”
As Mary Townsend wrote in Dolly Parton is Magnificent, Aristotle’s concept of kalos applies to Dolly: Something “good but also lovely, perfectly beautiful while astonishingly good, the kind of thing to aim for in word and deed that would never be boring, tired, or pedestrian; never merely a duty but always a pleasure.” This doesn’t go too far. Some were undoubtedly put off by her appearance, but as I remember it, she once broke up Johnny Carson when she said, “Honey, it takes a lot of money to look this cheap!” As Professor Stice notes in conclusion:
Somewhere someone is writing a piece explaining why Dolly Parton was not perfect and why many Americans are going too far in their idolization of her. Certainly no one is perfect and all human idols have feet of clay, but some people can still be exemplars. Dolly Parton pointed to what is possible, defying expectations and the excuses we often make for our own shortcomings. She is an example of human genius and generosity. In polarized times, she showed that it is still possible to be yourself without being polarizing. She showed that one can achieve success and enjoy it well and share it with family and community. It is possible to work hard and love what you do. It is possible to be a good citizen in your local and your national community. On Twitter, Miles Smith noted that the outpouring of grief over the loss of Dolly “is Appalachia’s version of the death of Queen Elizabeth.” Respectfully, that parallel may begin in Appalachia, but it extends to all of America. Dolly Parton achieved many things in her life, but one of her achievements was to become a national role model. Her legacy will continue, but her absence will be widely felt.
Amen. And last week I sent a contribution to her Imagination Library so that long into the future, another 300 million books, and more, will be distributed to young readers the world over.
Part the Second: Dolly Parton the Writer (and the Singer). More than thirty years ago, I wondered how many of those enamored with Whitney Houston’s version of “I Will Always Love You” knew the song was written by Dolly Parton as a gift to Porter Wagoner, whom she left to chart her own course. According to lore, Dolly Parton wrote over 3,000 songs. In Eagles Were Born to Fly, also in FPR, Michial Farmer has put together fifteen of her best. I listened to all of them, from her singing “Backwoods Barbie” to Bettye LaVette’s version of “Little Sparrow.” There is no accounting for taste, but these works of art represent pure genius, performed by others of genius, including Merle Haggard, Emmylou Harris, Margie Joseph, and Norah Jones. Enjoy!
Part the Third: The Wages of Industrial Agriculture Is Death. Back to another world, where things are less beautiful and sublime, but where Wendell Berry was right. The dead zone at the mouth of the Mississippi River continues to wax and wane throughout the year, as told in Mapping America’s Largest Dead Zone (archived). As longtime readers know, I grew up close to the ocean and in my childhood visited my father’s siblings at their home on the other estuary in Louisiana. The two were different, but incredibly productive, as anyone could see. The shrimp boats in both places returned with abundant catches of the most remarkable creatures. But things have changed, in both places:
On a sweltering night in late July, a team of scientists gathered onboard the R.V. Pelican in Houma, La., a 116-foot blue-and-white vessel resting in a bed of water hyacinths under a stormy sunset.
As the clock ticked toward their midnight castoff, the scientists raced to set up the last of their equipment in the ship’s small laboratories. For the next week, they would be working 24-hour days in tight quarters to measure what little oxygen was left in the Gulf of Mexico’s infamous dead zone.
The dead zone results from excess nutrients, mostly from fertilizers, running off farmland into the Mississippi River and finally into the Gulf. The size of the oxygen-starved zone changes every year, growing as more nutrients make their way into the Gulf and shrinking when tropical storms or strong currents mix the water.
…
Nutrients running from (industrial) farms into the Mississippi River are carried to the Gulf, where they encourage the growth of algae. It blooms and then dies, feeding bacteria that gobble up the water’s oxygen.
The long-running crisis endangers marine life and the livelihoods of thousands of shrimpers and fishers. The search for oxygen drives fish accustomed to life near the seafloor to venture higher into the water column, and bottom-dwelling creatures — like shrimp — to migrate to the dead zone’s edges.
This exodus of sea creatures leaves the top layers of the water vibrant and full of life, but the seafloor a practically barren muck.
The research these marine scientists do is essential, if only to mark devastation visited upon the natural world by human beings, said natural world including human beings, which is often forgotten during the Neoliberal Dispensation. But the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) has seen its budget cut by 44% during the Current Administration. Nothing to see here, move along. This is just more research that very clearly doesn’t dovetail with the “priorities” of the powers that be. And so it goes. And so will our damage willfully continue, as Southern Louisiana loses roughly one football field of land every 100 minutes. Seven football fields here and another seven there, every day, 365 days a year, and pretty soon we are talking about real loss.
Part the Fourth: Is Junk Food Addiction Real? Big Ag and Big Food will fairly shout, “No!” And it is true that opioids and opiates produce effects in the brain that processed foods do not. Nor is tolerance (the need to use a larger dose to achieve a similar effect) seen in studies of food addiction. But it is clear that Big Food has become a master at producing industrial food-like products that tickle the human bliss point for salt, sugar, and fat (highly recommended and common in used bookstores). And therein lies the problem. Whether addiction to ultra-processed food (UPF) is the “same” as addiction to heroin is immaterial if UPFs are manufactured to be habit forming. In an upcoming post I plan to write about the scientist who retired from NIH early before the Current Administration could fire him for insisting on making the distinction, in this case without much of a difference, between “addictive” and “habit forming.” Kevin Hall, now of the University of Ottawa, will be speaking at the 2026 Trottier Symposium at McGill University on September 29th. Any readers in and around Montreal are encouraged to attend. I will eventually watch the available video and report back.
Emily Shore has a good, short article in the McGill Office for Science and Society on The Junk Food Addiction:
Ever feel like you’re addicted to food? Not all food, of course, but junk food. The type of food that my kids negotiate to consume daily, despite doing my best to teach the benefits of proper nutrition. The very fact that these foods are referred to as “junk” connotes just how little they have to offer besides empty calories. What they do offer, as we all know, is taste. The type of taste that triggers our taste buds – and our brains – to want more. And more. And more… And for some individuals, the need to consume these foods is so great that the only way to stop thinking about them is to give in to the craving.
The concept of “food addiction” has become more mainstream recently due to the increased access and consumption of highly caloric, highly processed, and highly palatable foods. But the term “addiction”, in the context of food, is not new, tracing back to 1956, when allergist Theron Randolph first used it in connection with corn, wheat, coffee, milk, eggs, and potatoes. Today, the concept of “food addiction” is linked with foods that are mechanically processed, generally contain significant amounts of additives, and are typically high in calories, fats, salt, and sugar. Such -ultra-processed foods are low in nutritional value and are formulated to be so highly palatable that they become “addictive. While, like “junk food”, they are often low in nutritional quality, their distinguishing feature is the way in which they are manufactured and formulated. The term “ultra-processed” is a technical one.
…
The extent to which food producers have gone to produce hyperpalatable foods appealing to consumers’ taste buds has been likened by some to the same methods employed by tobacco companies to attract smokers.
And therein lies the other problem with our so-called “diet.” As with most of our other pressing problems, this one can be solved. Based on a fair amount of noise, this is a priority of the Current Administration. Whether they are serious, about the problem, that is, remains to be seen.
Part the Fifth: AI Meets Its Match. The current near-universal assumption is that algorithmic intelligence, broadly defined, will be a boon to all scientific research. I think this is correct, when the problem has boundaries that are understood and the training set is legitimate. For example, the development of AlphaFold has revolutionized the study of protein structure and function.
The protein folding problem has been a thing since Christian Anfinsen showed in 1961 that the amino acid sequence of bacterial ribonuclease (an enzyme that degrades RNA) is necessary, but not sufficient, to produce an active enzyme. The “but not sufficient” part is usually left out of the story told to students, and when I have brought this up in the presence of protein folders, they just give me that look that means, “Who left the door open and let the biologist in?”
Perhaps too much information, but Anfinsen produced functional enzyme in meaningful quantity only when he added small amounts of reducing agent to the solution containing the unfolded protein. This allowed the chain of amino acids to search conformational space, without reaching an irreversible dead end, and fold into the active enzyme. This reducing environment in the test tube mimicked the intracellular environment. Therefore, Anfinsen actually showed that an amino acid sequence needed no more genetic information to specify an active protein. The Central Dogma of Molecular Biology (DNA makes RNA makes protein) was only a few years old at the time, so this was the question at the forefront of molecular biology in 1961. The cellular inheritance present in every cell since the very first one appeared about three billion years ago is also an absolute requirement for the production of functional proteins. This is still forgotten, way too often.
Now, back to a story of biological function and AI. The bacterial virus ΦX174 was the first genome to be completely sequenced when I was an undergraduate, to universal acclaim. As much is known at the molecular level about ΦX174 as any other “organism.” And for this reason, the first viral genomes designed by AI were versions of ΦX174. Now researchers have “systematically mutated nearly every single nucleotide – another first for a full genome – and determined the consequences.”
Most of these mutations were detrimental to the virus’s survival, but for many of them, it was difficult to pinpoint why. “Even in this super well-studied system, we can’t explain why one-quarter of the mutations kill the virus,” says Ben Lehner, a molecular biologist at the Wellcome Sanger Institute in Hinxton, UK, who co-led the study, which was posted on the bioRxiv preprint server in July (NB: as a preprint, the paper has not yet been validated by peer review, to the extent that peer review is validation in the current world of pay-to-publish-anything).
Cutting-edge AI systems for biology research that have shown promise in identifying harmful mutations struggled to predict the effects of the changes in the phage. The findings underscore the need for more, and better, experimental data to power these biological-AI tools.
The Abstract from the preprint is worth reading in full:
The bacteriophage ΦX174 was the first genome to be sequenced and the first to be chemically synthesised. Here we present a complete map of the consequences of changing every nucleotide in the ΦX174 genome and every amino acid in the proteome. In total, half of nucleotide and >60% of amino acid changes impair fitness. However, this varies substantially across proteins and non-coding regions. Surprisingly, the most important mechanistic cause of reduced fitness is disruption of protein interaction interfaces, accounting for nearly half of detrimental protein variants. A further one quarter of damaging variants disrupt protein cores but one in four lack a mechanistic explanation. Mutational effects are only moderately-well predicted by state-of-the-art artificial intelligence models, but, combined with structural modelling, provide mechanistic hypotheses and insights into the DNA replication machinery. This complete mutagenesis of a biological system quantifies the limits of our current understanding of, and ability to predict, molecular biology.
So, what to say about this? My answer as the biologist in the room is that these scientists have left out three billion years of cell inheritance in their assumptions. “More, and better, experimental data” will not powerup these “biological-AI tools.” That “protein-protein interaction interfaces” represent the most important mechanism here is totally unsurprising. These interactions are the stuff of biological life, the cell inheritance that makes genetic inheritance possible, in the real world. Which came first, cell inheritance or genetic inheritance, is a question for late-night bull sessions in the lab. They are two legs of the three-legged stool essential for life, with the third being an environment that permits biological life in the first place. Which leg of a three-legged stool is most important is a nonsense question..
This brings us back to our near future with AI ruling our world. Cell inheritance, too complex for algorithmic intelligence now and probably forever, is the often undefined but very real ground truth of biological life. Similarly, institutional memory and knowledge of the workarounds that make useful work possible, except that done by robots in a completely determined environment, are the known but ignorable ground truths of cultural, social and, political life at every level. A “simple” virus infecting a “simple” cell is beyond the “ken” of AI. The complex life of individual human beings in society is most certainly beyond AI. The coming damage to be wrought by AI is inevitable, though, as the lords of the universe strive to turn us all into robotic serfs, but serfs for which they have no responsibility. Or, we can just say “No!” and make it stick.
Parting Shot: AI Still Makes Us Stupid but At Least We Will Sound Like One Another. Researchers worry that generative AI is homogenizing culture and cognition. That horse left the barn some time ago, and now scholars are worrying about it?
Emily Wenger, a computer scientist at Duke University in Durham, North Carolina, says the risk of homogenization is an existential one. “If we’re all using AI to write our e-mails or whatever, what do we become as a species?”
We might fall prey to groupthink, she warns. “We have suffered as a society when we silence or ignore edge voices.”
Whatever. Another thing, Professor Wenger: Edge voices, when they are not cancelled outright, are becoming illegal in a reprise of our various and sundry Red Scare hysterics, and this has had little to do with AI. However, AI diagnosis of pre-crime doesn’t seem to be too far beyond our horizon in a world of total information awareness.
On that note, thank you for reading! See you next week. For those of us in the United States, Happy Labor Day! Debout! les damnés de la terre! Debout! les forçats de la faim!

results.title: Flock says its cameras make US safer - so why are they being sabotaged?
results.author: Ellie House
results.content:
Flock says its cameras make US safer - so why are they being sabotaged?
Houston's historic Old Braeswood neighbourhood is affluent and tree-lined.
These are not the kind of streets where you would expect to see co-ordinated vandalism. Yet here, four surveillance cameras were attacked and cut down in the middle of the night.
The metal poles were severed, leaving the distinctive black oval cameras and accompanying solar panels lying on the ground. On some of the cameras was a red sign reading: "Notice. 24/7 video recording."
These cameras are run by a company called Flock Safety and this sabotage, which happened in late July, is a signal of growing concern over the nationwide spread of sophisticated AI-powered surveillance systems. Similar vandalism incidents have occurred in Minnesota, California and Georgia.
Proponents say they have made communities safer and have helped dramatically increase the rate at which crimes are solved. But recent examples of misuse have caused concern. Critics say the cameras, which take pictures of the rear of every car that drives past, are overly broad investigative tools that treat civilians like suspects.
They see the little black poles popping up in their neighbourhoods as visible reminders of state power, at a time when public confidence in institutions is historically low and many are concerned about the accelerating pace of technological change and the influence of AI on people's lives.
A new age of surveillance
Founded in 2017, Flock Safety has become one of the country's biggest makers of Automatic Licence Plate Readers (ALPRs). These AI-powered cameras take a picture of the rear of every car that drives past. Footage is retained for a specified amount of time.
But little is known about the extent to which Flock is being used - the company does not publish exact data, but says it works with more than 7,000 communities nationwide and estimates that there are approximately 100,000 cameras deployed.
Records obtained by the BBC provide a rare glimpse into the extensive network of cameras and surveillance tech being used in America's fourth largest city, Houston, including the use of controversial facial recognition software powered by artificial intelligence.
Flock is not just selling cameras - it is selling access to a database that can include thousands of cameras from around the country. Older ALPRs did not have this vast network, which is a major selling point for law enforcement.
For example, Houston's Metro Transit Authority owns 35 cameras. But documents show Metro has access to around 20,000 devices in the Flock network - including some as far as Albany County, New York.
And as Flock expands, so too can the scope of investigations. Documents released to the BBC show how the network has grown year-on-year. In the Cypress-Fairbanks independent school district, a typical licence plate lookup in April 2024 searched around 270 networks of cameras.
By April 2025, the typical search scope had almost doubled to around 500 networks. In April 2026, 20% of searches were conducted across more than 6,000 networks.
Critics in Houston say this national network concerns them more than individual cameras. Christopher Rivera, from the Texas Civil Rights Project, worries that authorities could use "these databases to search our everyday routines, which ultimately scrapes out our routes to work, where our children go to school, and where we worship - and that's very problematic".
There have been recent incidents of privacy breaches that have caught national attention. Last week, a police officer in Kentucky was charged after using the Flock system to track his ex-girlfriend - who filed a protection order - over 2,000 times.
He was caught using Flock's newly mandatory, AI-powered audit tool that flags suspicious use.
Others are concerned about Flock being a way for police to avoid warrants, which are usually required to search a person's property or tap their phone. In 2025, a detective in Johnson County, Texas, searched over 80,000 images to locate a woman suspected of having an abortion. He did not have a warrant.
CCTV cameras, licence-plate readers and surveillance are not new. But the scale of Flock's network and the integration of AI in modern surveillance tech is a recent development and it's turned Flock into a household name. Americans who otherwise ignored the cameras in their cities have started to notice and tune into the capabilities of the technology around them.
With AI, unlike older licence-plate readers, law enforcement can search surveillance footage with a string of words like "Caucasian man, blue shirt" - not just a licence-plate image.
One thing Flock does not use is facial recognition. But that does not mean police departments are avoiding that tech. Critics say it violates human rights, is susceptible to misidentifying innocent people, and can be biased against minorities.
The BBC has received documents revealing that Harris County Sheriff's Office, which covers Houston, uses other facial recognition technology, Clearview AI.
The tool includes a database of more than 70 billion images, many of which were scraped from public internet sources including social media. The documents, including purchase orders and a licence agreement, show that the county's Clearview AI contract currently runs through to March 2027.
Several European countries have issued the company with data protection fines, including a £7.5m penalty from the UK's Information Commissioner.
Harris County Sheriff's Office use of this facial recognition technology has not been reported before. It did not respond to requests for comment.
Police say surveillance technology like this, including Flock cameras, is important for fighting crime.
"It's a very good tool," says Chief Ray Schultz of the Memorial Villages Police Department - a small jurisdiction within Houston. "It makes the community safer."
Before purchasing a Flock ALPR, his department would recover an average of three stolen cars a year. Now, this figure is 45, Schultz says.
Some crimes solved in recent years would have been "impossible" without Flock, he adds. Last month, Schultz used the tool to find an elderly woman with dementia who had driven 60 miles from Galveston to Houston and had gotten lost. "We were able to find her and reunite her with her family."
Schultz says that it is important for agencies to have strong policies governing ALPR use and officers that misuse the system should be held accountable.
"But don't throw out a tool that is valuable, that can help recover a missing child."
'I feel like I'm being stalked'
Jasmine Khadem Gonzalez, an immigrant rights organiser, is worried that law enforcement might "use [the Flock] database to tell ICE where somebody is".
The federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency does not have a contract with Flock directly. However, there have been reports of police officers citing "immigration" or "ice" as a reason for searching for a licence plate.
Jessie, an immigrant from Central America, noticed a Flock camera outside her house last month. She asked the BBC to not use her real name out of fear it could impact a pending case to extend her green card.
"It makes me feel as if I'm being stalked," she says.
In response, she's changed her commute to work. "I try to take different routes every day so there's not a pattern."
But whether individual law enforcement agencies share info with the federal government is unclear. Federal immigration enforcement cannot access Flock data directly, Flock's CEO says. But some police departments have standing agreements with federal immigration enforcement to work together.
In Harris County, a proposed Flock contract amendment initially included the explicit authorisation to share camera data with federal law enforcement, but this provision was later removed after push-back from campaigners.
Hundreds of contracts cancelled
Some jurisdictions have opted not to renew contracts with Flock as a result of these concerns, including large metropolitan areas like Los Angeles, Seattle and Austin.
In total, more than 200 communities have cancelled or not renewed their contracts since 2021 - including 90 in August alone - according to advocacy group Secure Justice. Their reasons for cancelling may include cost and concerns about data privacy.
Nationally, lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have suggested that there ought to be guardrails and several candidates have made it a campaign issue for the upcoming midterms. Republican Congressman Keith Self has proposed legislation that would require federal agencies to get warrants before accessing Flock data.
The company itself has also amended some of its policies, such as requiring mandatory audits and reducing the default period that data stays on a server from 30 days to seven, unless flagged as part of an investigation. But individual agencies can choose to retain data for much longer.
Flock's founder and CEO Garrett Langley told the BBC that it was up to individual cities to decide how long to store data and what information to share with whom.
"I don't think a technology company should be making decisions like that," he says.
"As long as it's a lawful investigation, we are not going to tell cities what laws they should or should not enforce."
Flock is a safety, not surveillance, company, Langley says. Yet three patents filed between 2020 and 2025 have the word "surveillance" in the title.
He boasts that the tech helped solve "about a million crimes" and helped find more than 10,000 missing people.
"The debate of how we build a society where safety and privacy coexist" is worth having, he says, but the ongoing vandalism is "disappointing".
But there is nothing Flock or law enforcement could say to make Jessie feel at ease with this technology, she says. "I just don't trust that they're doing it to keep us safe."
results.summary:
Rising vandalism against Flock Safety cameras reflects growing public anxiety over the rapid expansion of AI-powered surveillance networks and their potential for misuse by law enforcement agencies nationwide.

### Key Points
- Flock Safety operates approximately 100,000 AI-powered Automatic Licence Plate Readers (ALPRs) across more than 7,000 communities in the United States.
- The company’s network allows law enforcement to search vast databases of vehicle movements, with some search scopes expanding to cover thousands of camera networks.
- Privacy advocates and critics express concern over the lack of warrants for data access, potential for stalking, and the tracking of sensitive daily routines.
- Reports indicate that some police departments, including the Harris County Sheriff's Office, also utilize Clearview AI facial recognition software to supplement surveillance efforts.
- Over 200 jurisdictions have cancelled or declined to renew Flock contracts since 2021 due to mounting concerns regarding data privacy, costs, and civil liberties.

### Why it Matters
The proliferation of these surveillance tools highlights a fundamental tension between public safety initiatives and individual privacy rights in the digital age. As law enforcement agencies increasingly rely on interconnected AI databases, the lack of standardized federal oversight has sparked a national debate over the necessity of legal guardrails to prevent systemic abuse.
